prompt: A service on a 32-core machine replaces a mutex around a hash-map lookup with a `pthread_rwlock_t`. Lookups take about 100 ns and make up 99.9% of operations. Throughput barely improves. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: `pthread_rwlock_rdlock` makes a system call every time, so readers are slow
options.explanation: Like mutexes, glibc's rwlocks take a user-space fast path with atomic instructions when they can. The cost here is not syscalls.
A low write count does not alone rule out long writer hold times. The question illustrates reader-metadata contention as a plausible cause; measurement must distinguish it from writer delays.

options.text: glibc read-write locks only let one reader in at a time
options.explanation: Readers do share the lock. The problem is what each reader has to do to get in.

options.text: A plausible cause is coherence traffic from shared reader-metadata updates dominating the short useful lookup
options.explanation: Correct as a hypothesis to test. Many read-write-lock implementations update shared reader metadata, so short reads can spend much of their time on coherence traffic. The hypothetical lookup duration and write percentage do not prove that this is the measured bottleneck.

workedExample: A plausible bottleneck is atomic modification of shared rwlock metadata on reader entry/exit. That coherence traffic can dominate very short useful work. The hypothetical 100 ns lookup is not a measured cache-transfer latency, and write frequency alone does not prove writer hold times are harmless. Profile the implementation before choosing RCU, sharding or another protocol.
